strongest_rejected_alternative: The 7:11-36 precedent (one zot-torat superscription split into five occasion-based chunks) might seem to argue for splitting ch.12 too, but that precedent is distinguishable: 7:11ff is followed by multiple fresh protases marking genuinely distinct occasions, while ch.12 contains only one internal transition within a single, tightly unified case, closed by a colophon that explicitly names both halves as one torah.
boundary_evidence_refs: oshb:Lev.12.7 זֹאת תּוֹרַת הַיֹּלֶדֶת לַזָּכָר אוֹ לַנְּקֵבָה (single-witness, carries the merge alone)

oshb:Lev.7.11, 7.16, 7.19 (single-witness, the distinguishing multiple-fresh-protases precedent)

boundary_rationale: A means-tested protasis, 'if she cannot afford a lamb,' opens a poor-alternative provision matching the graduated-offering pattern already established in 5:7-13, substituting two birds for the lamb-plus-bird combination just prescribed.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reviewer could fold this one-verse alternative back into the preceding offering-and-colophon unit rather than isolating it; I kept it separate for consistency with how ch.5's and ch.14's poor-provision alternatives are each given their own chunk on the strength of their own conditional opening, even though this is among the thinnest units in the book.

boundary_rationale: A fresh joint messenger formula to Moses and Aaron opens the diagnostic case-series torah, and the first case, marked by its own protasis 'when a man shall have a swelling in his body's skin,' establishes the chapter's basic examine-isolate-reexamine procedure before any of the specialized sub-cases that follow.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could treat the whole of vv.1-46 as a single undifferentiated 'skin disease' unit, since the examine/isolate/pronounce procedure repeats throughout; I split at each new casuistic protasis instead, since each names a distinct triggering condition (swelling, chronic disease, boils, burns, scalp/beard, bright spots, baldness) and the owner addendum treats a syntactic protasis/apodosis as tier-1 boundary-driving evidence.

boundary_rationale: A new protasis, 'when the plague of leprosy is in a man,' opens the case of an already-advanced condition (raw flesh visible, no isolation required since uncleanness is certain), which the text itself extends without a further protasis break into the further extreme case of leprosy covering the entire body turning wholly white.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A finer split could separate the chronic case (9-11) from the all-over-white case (12-17) at v.12's 'if the leprosy breaks out all over the skin'; I kept them merged since v.12 continues describing the same referent (a man already diagnosed with the disease of vv.9-11) rather than opening a fresh, independent triggering condition.

boundary_rationale: A new protasis, 'when the body has a boil on its skin, and it has healed,' opens a distinct diagnostic case addressing scar tissue from a specific prior wound-type, closed on its own clean-verdict formula.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the burn-scar case immediately following it, since both address disease breaking out in a healed wound; but each opens with its own triggering wound-type (boil versus fire-burn) and the book consistently marks each new protasis as a fresh case throughout this chapter.

boundary_rationale: A parallel protasis, 'or when the body has a burn from fire on its skin,' opens the burn-scar case, matching the boil-scar case's structure (raw flesh in the wound becomes a bright spot, examine, isolate if uncertain, pronounce) but triggered by a different wound-type.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A minimal reading could merge this with the boil-scar case as 'wound-scar diseases generally,' since the procedure is nearly identical; I kept them separate because the text's own connective, 'or when,' explicitly marks this as a distinct triggering condition rather than a continuation.

boundary_rationale: A new protasis addressing a new class of participant, 'when a man or woman has a plague on the head or on the beard,' opens the scalp/beard case (netek), distinguished procedurally by yellow rather than white hair as the diagnostic marker and by shaving as part of the isolation procedure.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could fold this into the preceding burn-scar case as a further sub-variety of skin disease; but this case explicitly introduces the first mention of women as potential subjects and a body location (head/beard) never addressed before, together with a diagnostic marker (yellow hair) unique to this case.

boundary_rationale: A brief protasis, 'when a man or a woman has bright spots in the skin of the body,' opens a case whose entire content is a clean verdict for a harmless rash (bohaq), the shortest and simplest of the chapter's diagnostic cases.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the baldness case that follows, since both are brief benign-condition verdicts without an isolation procedure; but each opens with its own protasis addressing a distinct bodily phenomenon (skin bright spots versus hair loss), and I judged the formula break, though short, worth preserving rather than collapsing two textually distinct conditions into one chunk.

boundary_rationale: A new protasis, 'if a man's hair has fallen from his head, he is bald,' opens the baldness case, immediately distinguishing ordinary natural baldness (clean) from disease breaking out within a bald area (unclean), a two-part case with its own internal contrast.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reader could treat ordinary baldness (40-41) and diseased baldness (42-44) as two separate chunks, matching the fine granularity used for scalp/beard sub-cases elsewhere; I kept them merged since v.42's 'but if' is a direct contrastive continuation of the same bodily condition just introduced, not an independent new triggering event.

boundary_rationale: The discourse shifts from diagnostic casuistry to an apodictic behavioral mandate for anyone diagnosed a leper -- torn clothes, loose hair, the covered lip, the 'unclean, unclean' cry, and dwelling alone outside the camp -- functioning as a coda that closes the human skin-disease portion of the chapter before the register shifts entirely to fabric and leather.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be tacked onto the baldness case immediately before it as its closing application; but its content applies to every diagnosed leper regardless of which specific case produced the diagnosis, making it a generalizing coda for vv.1-44 as a whole rather than a continuation of the baldness case specifically.

boundary_rationale: A new substrate opens the chapter's final case, 'the garment also that the plague of leprosy is in,' shifting from human skin to woolen, linen, or leather material entirely, and running through its own examine-isolate-burn-or-wash procedure to the chapter's own zot torat colophon at v.59.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A finer split could separate the initial diagnosis (47-52) from the wash-and-reexamine procedure (53-58) and the colophon (59), matching the granularity used for human skin cases earlier; I kept the whole garment case together because, unlike the human cases, there is no fresh casuistic protasis reopening the topic partway through -- the whole span describes one continuous examination-and-disposition procedure for a single kind of object.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.13.47 "The garment also that the plague of leprosy is in"

boundary_rationale: WLC 14:3-7 is a single unbroken הכהן-subject chain (וְצִוָּה הַכֹּהֵן repeats at v.4 and v.5) with no tier-1 signal -- no fresh protasis, no addressee shift, no new participant -- falling at 14:4. V.6 varies this chain stylistically with a fronted-object construction, אֶת הַצִּפֹּר הַֽחַיָּה יִקַּח אֹתָהּ ('the living bird -- he shall take it'), a yiqtol rather than a strict verb-initial weqatal; the fronting foregrounds the ritual object for emphasis and does not introduce a new subject, protasis, or participant, so it does not constitute a tier-1 boundary signal and the chain's functional continuity from v.3 through v.7 is unaffected.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The introduction of new ritual objects at v.4 (two birds, cedar wood, scarlet, hyssop) might look like grounds for a fresh unit, but that warrant is applied nowhere else in this cluster and was explicitly disavowed for comparable object-introductions elsewhere in ch.13-14's own case material.

boundary_rationale: The subject shifts from the priest's actions to the cleansed person's own required actions -- washing clothes, shaving all hair, bathing -- performed first on day one and repeated on day seven, forming a distinct two-stage personal-purification interval before the offerings of the eighth day.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be folded into the two-bird rite as its immediate aftermath; but the two-bird rite is performed entirely by the priest upon the person, while this unit shifts to actions the person performs upon himself across a seven-day interval, a genuine change in agency and timeframe.

strongest_rejected_alternative: A finer split could separate the trespass-offering blood/oil application (12-18) from the sin- and burnt-offering conclusion (19-20); I kept them merged since no new object or participant is introduced between them, and the entire sequence is bound together as the one ceremony performed 'before Yahweh' on this single eighth day.

strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be treated as a mere footnote appended to the full-offering unit; but it is a complete, independently structured procedure (its own lamb, its own oil measure, its own bird-substitution) sealed by its own colophon, exactly the kind of self-contained unit the book elsewhere gives its own chunk.

strongest_rejected_alternative: One might see this as a straightforward continuation of the leper-cleansing torah just concluded, since both concern purity diagnosis; but the fresh messenger formula and the shift to an entirely new substrate (dwelling structures) mark this as its own torah, matching how garment mildew was separated from human skin disease in ch.13.

boundary_rationale: 16:11's near-verbatim repetition of 16:6 (וְהִקְרִיב אַהֲרֹן אֶת פַּר הַחַטָּאת אֲשֶׁר לוֹ וְכִפֶּר בַּעֲדוֹ וּבְעַד בֵּיתוֹ) is classical resumptive repetition (Wiederaufnahme): a proleptic summary at v.6, an inserted digression required by the larger procedure (vv.7-10, the goat-lot casting, structurally necessary before v.15 can name 'the goat of the sin offering for the people'), and a verbatim-repetition resumption at v.11 that continues the interrupted action -- וְשָׁחַט אֶת פַּר הַחַטָּאת אֲשֶׁר לוֹ, the concrete slaughter the v.6 summary had only announced -- through the coals, incense, and sevenfold blood-sprinkling of vv.12-14. This device marks continuation of one interrupted unit across the digression, not the opening of a second independent one.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The near-verbatim repetition at 16:11 could be read as a fresh unit-opening signal in its own right (a plausible surface reading of 'resumptive repetition' as a boundary marker), but that inverts the device's actual function: Wiederaufnahme brackets an interrupting digression to signal that the bracketed material completes the same statement, not that it restarts a new one. The real, stronger seam is v.15's new sacrificial object (שְׂעִיר הַחַטָּאת אֲשֶׁר לָעָם, explicitly contrasted with the אֲשֶׁר לוֹ of vv.6/11) and new beneficiary, where the atonement's scope visibly widens from the mercy seat alone to the Holy Place, Tent, and altar.

boundary_rationale: This unit opens on the same אָז-plus-land-subject-shift signal that closes M8-Lev-168 (see that decision), the genuine Hebrew marker of a new descriptive proposition; an internal sub-seam recurs at v.36/v.39 (וְהַנִּשְׁאָרִים בָּכֶם, repeated), correctly treated as internal structure within this one unit rather than grounds to shrink its outer boundary.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Rescoping this unit to begin at v.36 (matching its 'survivors' terror' content and a real WEB paragraph break there) was proposed, with 26:34-35 folded into M8-Lev-168 instead as that tier's causal outworking; but the paragraph-break evidence is metadata-only, and the אָז-plus-land-subject signal at v.34 is the stronger, evidence-rule-privileged marker for this unit's actual start. Preserved on record as a considered alternative, not adopted.

boundary_rationale: V.40, וְהִתְוַדּוּ אֶת עֲוֺנָם וְאֶת עֲוֺן אֲבֹתָם, is a waw-consecutive perfect continuing v.39's 3mp chain (יִמַּקּוּ), not a marked conditional; the original 'if they confess' framing was a WEB interpretive rendering with no oshb ref actually tested against it. The seam at 26:39/40 is retained but re-grounded on the real Hebrew markers instead: the אוֹ אָז discourse pivot at v.41 (אוֹ אָז יִכָּנַע לְבָבָם הֶעָרֵל) and the וְזָכַרְתִּי covenant-remembrance chain recurring at vv.42 and 45.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The seam itself could be abandoned along with the mistaken 'protasis' framing, folding vv.40-45 back into the preceding tier-five/exile material as one continuous 3mp chain; but the אוֹ אָז pivot and the repeated covenant-remembrance formula are real, checkable turns in the discourse that justify keeping this as its own restoration unit, just not on the conditional-clause ground originally claimed.

boundary_rationale: A summary colophon closes the entire legislative corpus reaching back to the beginning of the book, 'these are the statutes, ordinances, and laws, which Yahweh made between him and the children of Israel in Mount Sinai by Moses,' the most comprehensive of the book's colophons in scope.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be attached to the restoration unit as its closing verse; but its retrospective, whole-corpus-summarizing language (naming three distinct categories of law and dating them all to Sinai) matches the colophon function seen at 7:37-38 and 11:46-47 exactly, marking it as its own closing unit for the whole Sinai legislation rather than a continuation of ch.26's blessing/curse material specifically.

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger formula opens the book's final appendix, explicitly outside the Sinai-corpus colophon just given at 26:46, addressing vows to dedicate a person's value to Yahweh, with a graduated fee schedule by age and sex closing on a means-tested provision for the poor matching the pattern of similar provisions in chs.5, 12, and 14.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could read the whole chapter as continuing the legal material of chs.1-26 without a real break; but the closing colophon at 26:46 explicitly marks the end of 'the statutes...which Yahweh made...in Mount Sinai,' and ch.27's fresh messenger formula opens genuinely new subject matter (personal and property vows) not covered by anything preceding it, functioning as a recognized appendix.

web:Lev.27.8 "if he is poorer than your valuation...The priest shall assign a value according to his ability to pay"

boundary_rationale: A new protasis, 'if it is an animal of which men offer an offering to Yahweh,' shifts the vow object from a person to an animal, introducing a distinct substitution rule (any exchange, good for bad, renders both animals holy) not applicable to the person-valuation case.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the person-valuation unit as 'vows generally'; but the valuation mechanism itself changes entirely -- persons are priced by a fixed age/sex schedule, while animals are subject to a substitution-penalty rule with no fixed schedule at all -- marking a genuine functional break.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.27.9 "If it is an animal of which men offer an offering to Yahweh"
web:Lev.27.10 "if he shall at all exchange animal for animal, then both it and that for which it is exchanged shall be holy"

boundary_rationale: A new protasis, 'when a man dedicates his house to be holy to Yahweh,' opens a third vow-object category, houses, with its own priestly-evaluation-plus-redemption mechanism distinct from both the person and animal cases.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One might fold this into the animal-substitution unit as 'more property vows'; but a house is evaluated and redeemed by an entirely different procedure (priestly appraisal plus a fifth added for redemption, with no substitution concept at all), matching the book's pattern of treating each new vow-object as its own case.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.27.14 "When a man dedicates his house to be holy to Yahweh, then the priest shall evaluate it"
web:Lev.27.15 "he shall add the fifth part of the money of your valuation to it, and it shall be his"

boundary_rationale: A new protasis, 'if a man dedicates to Yahweh part of the field of his possession,' opens the fourth vow-object category, ancestral land, with a valuation mechanism explicitly tied to the Jubilee cycle (seed-yield pricing, redemption windows scaled to years remaining) not present in any of the preceding cases.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the house-dedication unit as 'more real-property vows'; but the field's valuation is explicitly anchored to the Jubilee calendar established in ch.25, an entirely different pricing logic from the flat priestly appraisal used for houses, and the field case is substantially longer and more elaborate.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.27.16 "If a man dedicates to Yahweh part of the field of his possession"
web:Lev.27.17 "If he dedicates his field from the Year of Jubilee, according to your valuation it shall stand"

boundary_rationale: A contrasting protasis, 'if he dedicates a field to Yahweh which he has bought, which is not of the field of his possession,' opens a distinct sub-case for purchased (rather than ancestral) land, whose Jubilee-year disposition differs sharply -- it reverts to the original owner rather than becoming the dedicator's own permanent holding.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reader might treat this as a mere footnote to the ancestral-field unit rather than its own chunk; but the outcome at Jubilee is categorically different between the two field types (permanent priestly holding for ancestral land devoted outright, versus reversion to the original owner for purchased land), a distinction significant enough that the text opens this case with its own explicit contrast.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.27.22 "if he dedicates a field to Yahweh which he has bought"
web:Lev.27.24 "In the Year of Jubilee the field shall return to him from whom it was bought"

boundary_rationale: A restrictive clause, 'however the firstborn among animals, which belongs to Yahweh as a firstborn, no man may dedicate,' opens a brief exclusion rule -- firstborn animals already belong to Yahweh by an earlier claim and so cannot be freshly vowed -- a distinct legal point from the field-valuation cases just concluded.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the purchased-field case as 'more valuation exceptions'; but its logic is different in kind (a prior claim precluding a fresh vow, not a valuation-and-redemption schedule), and its opening adversative 'however' (akh) explicitly marks it as a new restriction rather than a continuation.

boundary_rationale: A new protasis, 'no devoted thing that a man devotes to Yahweh...shall be sold or redeemed,' introduces cherem (irrevocable devotion), the vow appendix's most absolute category, explicitly contrasted with every preceding case by its total exclusion of redemption -- extending in v.29 to the case of a person devoted to destruction, who cannot be ransomed at all.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A finer split could separate the general devoted-things rule (28) from the human-cherem case (29); I merged them because both share the same absolute no-redemption logic and the human case reads as the most extreme instance of the general principle just stated rather than an independently triggered new topic.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.27.28 "Everything that is permanently devoted is most holy to Yahweh"
web:Lev.27.29 "No one devoted to destruction...shall be ransomed. He shall surely be put to death"

boundary_rationale: A new topic opens, 'all the tithe of the land...is Yahweh's,' shifting from vow-and-dedication law (a voluntary act) to the tithe (a standing obligation), covering both agricultural produce and livestock passing under the shepherd's rod, with its own redemption-plus-a-fifth mechanism for produce but an explicit no-substitution rule for livestock.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the devoted-things unit as 'more holy-property rules'; but the tithe is conceptually distinct from a vow or cherem -- it is a regular, obligatory portion rather than a special dedication -- and the chapter itself signals the shift with a fresh topic-opening clause rather than continuing the cherem logic.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.27.30 "All the tithe of the land, whether of the seed of the land or of the fruit of the trees, is Yahweh's"
web:Lev.27.32 "All the tithe of the herds or the flocks, whatever passes under the rod, the tenth shall be holy to Yahweh"

boundary_rationale: A final colophon closes both the vow appendix and the whole book, 'these are the commandments which Yahweh commanded Moses for the children of Israel on Mount Sinai,' explicitly echoing the 'Mount Sinai' bookend of 7:38, 25:1, and 26:46 one last time to frame the entirety of Leviticus as Sinai-given legislation.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be attached to the tithe-law unit as its closing verse; but its retrospective, whole-book-summarizing language and its explicit dating formula match the function of every other colophon in the book rather than the specific content of the tithe law just given, marking it as the book's own final closing frame.
